summary.title: Design Patterns and Refactoring
summary.one_liner: You learn what software design patterns are, the classic creational, structural and behavioral pattern catalog (Gang of Four style), and the main criticisms of the pattern concept.
takeaways: A design pattern is a general, reusable template for solving a common software design problem, not finished code.
Patterns fall into three groups: creational (object instantiation), structural (class and object composition) and behavioral (communication between objects).
Each pattern gets a one-line description, e.g. Singleton (only one instance can exist) and Observer (notifying change to a number of classes).
The page lists criticisms: patterns may target the wrong problem, lack formal foundations, can lead to inefficient code, and differ little from other abstractions.
summary.summary: This SourceMaking page introduces software design patterns as repeatable, documented solutions to common design problems and explains their benefits for development speed and communication. It then catalogs the classic Gang of Four patterns in three groups (creational, structural, behavioral), giving a one-line description for each. The page closes with a criticism section that cites Paul Graham and Peter Norvig, notes the lack of formal foundations, and argues that patterns can duplicate code and resemble other abstractions. The page text provides short descriptions only; code examples are mentioned in the meta description (Java, C++, C#, PHP, Delphi) but are not in the text given.
